ch28.note: A picul (Chinese dan, 担) is a traditional unit of weight of about sixty kilograms (133 pounds), the standard measure for bulk grain—so a reward reckoned in piculs of rice fixes its value in the one commodity that held its worth through the inflation of the war years.

Hongkou (Hongkew), the district north of Suzhou Creek, was the Japanese quarter of Shanghai and the seat of their garrison—their 'Little Tokyo.' To carry out a killing there, deep in enemy ground, is the measure of the operation's daring.
The Special Naval Landing Forces (海軍陸戦隊, Rikusentai), Japan's naval infantry or 'marines,' headquartered in Hongkou; they were the main Japanese fighting force inside Shanghai.

The Hanyeping Company (汉冶萍), China's largest early modern heavy-industry combine, uniting the Hanyang ironworks, the Daye iron mines, and the Pingxiang colliery. To have run it marks a man as a magnate of the first rank.

A comprador (买办, maiban) was the Chinese manager who served as the local agent and go-between for a foreign firm or bank. The type—part official, part comprador—grew rich off the foreign presence and was scorned by nationalists as battening on it.

ch28.anchor: the fox grieving over the dead hare
ch28.note: The idiom tu si hu bei (兔死狐悲), 'the hare dead, the fox grieves': to mourn the fate of one of one's own kind, half in fellow-feeling and half in fear of sharing it—said here with an edge of the collaborators' cold self-interest.

ch28.anchor: Sun Sun, Dah Sun, Wing On, Sincere
ch28.note: The four great Cantonese-run department stores of Nanjing Road—Sincere, Wing On, Sun Sun, and Dah Sun (The Sun)—the flagship emporiums of modern Shanghai, whose crowds made them useful ground for a covert meeting or a public killing.

The Federal Reserve Bank of China, the note-issuing bank of the Japanese-backed North China puppet regime (set up 1938); its notes were the occupation money of the north. It has nothing to do with the American institution of the same English name.
